text.p: The United States condemned on Thursday a Serbian crackdown on anti-government protesters and said it was continuing to hold President Slobodan Milosevic responsible for any violence.

"We repeat our call on the Serbian authorities to show restraint and to not interfere with the protesters' democratic rights," a State Department spokesman said. "We continue to hold Milosevic responsible for any violence which may occur."

In Belgrade, riot police forced opposition demonstrators off the streets on Thursday to enforce an Interior Ministry ban on marches. The marches by supporters of the Zajedno opposition parties had gone on for five weeks without violence until Tuesday, when Milosevic's ruling Socialist Party organised a counter-demonstration that touched off street fighting.

The State Department blasted the new restrictions on the anti-government protests as "an attempt to prevent the marchers from exercising their rights (that) can only serve to increase the possibility of confrontation and violence."

Asked how the United States could hold Milosevic responsible in advance for any violence, John Dinger, a department spokesman, told reporters: "What we've seen is 36, 37 days of ... peaceful demonstrations. They only became violent through the provocative and irresponsible actions of the Serbian government" when it organised the counter-demontration on Tuesday.

"It is pretty easy to draw the conclusion that if there's violence, it's going to be the result of irresponsible, provocative actions by the Serbian government," he said. "I think it's quite easy to draw the conclusion we've drawn."

After street fighting erupted on Tuesday, Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott warned Milosevic in effect that he faced economic reprisals and continued international isolation if he unleased his security forces to crush dissent.
The anti-government protests began after Milosevic refused to accept opposition victories in local elections on Nov. 17.
In Belgrade, Milosevic rejcted a request for an emergency meeting with the top U.S. diplomat in Serbia, Richard Miles, who saw Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic instead.
